author: Magistra Ottilie Vane, Society of Antiquarians
pages:
#The Question

Under the mountains of the north lie cities of bronze and stone, lit by lamps that still burn after uncounted centuries. Their builders, the Dwemer, called by some the deep elves and by others the dwarves, are gone. Not dead in any battle we know of. Not fled to any land we have found. Simply gone.

This essay surveys the leading theories, and gently mocks most of them.

#Theory the First: They Left

Some scholars hold that the Dwemer departed through some great gate or vessel, to another world entirely. They point to the vast chambers found in several ruins, too large for any purpose but launching something enormous.

The difficulty is that the Dwemer left behind their tools, their coins, half-eaten meals and, in one memorable case, a bath still full of water. Travellers do not usually leave the bath running.

#Theory the Second: They Were Destroyed

Others say the Dwemer meddled with powers beyond their understanding and were unmade in an instant. The machines that still guard their halls, these scholars argue, are simply carrying on without masters, like a mill wheel that keeps turning after the miller has died.

This theory is grim but tidy. It explains the abandoned meals. It does not explain why there are no bones.

#Theory the Third: They Are Still There

A small and noisy group insists the Dwemer never left at all, but merely retreated deeper, below the deepest ruins we have explored. Every strange noise from a mine shaft is taken as proof.

I have personally visited eleven Dwemer ruins. I have heard many strange noises. All of them, so far, were made by the machines, the spiders, or my own assistants.

#My Own View

I do not know where the Dwemer went. I suspect they did not know either, at the end. Whatever they attempted, it happened faster than anyone could write it down.

What I do know is this: their machines still work, still guard and still strike. Whatever the Dwemer were, they built to last. Do not go into their halls expecting an empty museum.
